assessment.nobel_worthiness: Opening a new observational window: IceCube's detection of a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos at TeV-PeV energies, and the later association with a flaring blazar, created neutrino astronomy as a working discipline. The achievement is as much instrumental as scientific, instrumenting a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice at the South Pole, which is exactly the kind of detector-driven discovery I weigh heavily as an astroparticle experimentalist.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and drove the cubic-kilometre concept and led the collaboration, and Karle was central to the AMANDA-to-IceCube development, construction and the detection effort. Spiering is credited too and was important in early neutrino-telescope work, but the decisive pair for IceCube itself seems to be Halzen and Karle. The wider lineage (Baikal, DUMAND, AMANDA, ANTARES) is not among the credited names and could complicate a fair allocation.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse astrophysical flux is confirmed at high significance and by independent analyses, and the galactic-plane neutrino emission has also been reported. Source identification is still partial (the TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 evidence is at moderate significance), but the discovery claim itself is stable and the recognition would be timely.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wants the prize anchored on the diffuse-flux discovery or waits for firmer source identification.
Credit among IceCube leaders and the precursor projects is not fully settled; I cannot independently verify the details of internal credit.
I am relying on my background knowledge of the results rather than independent verification.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and demonstrated to reach fractional uncertainty near 1e-18, redefined the limits of frequency metrology. They are enabling tools for tests of fundamental constants, searches for dark-matter signatures, relativistic geodesy and a future redefinition of the second. The idea is original, the realisation clear, and the impact lasting.
assessment.attribution: Katori invented the magic-wavelength lattice concept and first realised strontium lattice clocks; Jun Ye brought the performance to the systematic frontier and showed many-body clock physics. A two-person split is clean and the supplied credit supports it directly.
assessment.maturity: Mature: multiple independent laboratories confirm the performance and the international metrology community is moving toward redefinition. Recognition is timely and arguably slightly overdue, given that the 2005 and 2012 prizes covered adjacent but different steps (frequency combs, ion control).
uncertainties: Contributions from ion-clock groups and from earlier lattice and comb work could be argued as part of a broader prize.
Whether the committee judges this as precision engineering or as a discovery-class advance.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators, in theory and in the HgTe experiment, introduced a new classification of electronic phases of matter, with a rich consequent literature on topological materials. The conceptual originality and breadth are high, and the experimental realisation closes the loop between prediction and measurement.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele proposed the Z2 topological classification and the quantum spin Hall effect in graphene; Molenkamp's group experimentally observed the effect in HgTe wells following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. The BHZ theorists (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) are not among the credited names, which leaves a fairness problem within the supplied list, though a prize with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is defensible within the exact credited strings. The three-dimensional topological insulator work (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore and Balents; Hasan; Zhang) is also absent.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: robust independent confirmation across materials, and a vast follow-up literature. The 2016 prize on topological phase transitions (Thouless, Haldane, Kosterlitz) already acknowledged topology in matter, so this would be a clear follow-on rather than premature.
uncertainties: Credit gaps from the BHZ proposal and the three-dimensional topological insulator discoveries.
Overlap with the other topological-insulator entry on this list (B049) means the committee must pick one framing.
Practical applications remain limited so far, though that is not a prize criterion.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation of strongly correlated matter with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, including the superfluid-Mott insulator transition, fermionic Hubbard physics and single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopes, made it possible to engineer and probe many-body Hamiltonians with a control that solid-state systems cannot offer. The scientific footprint is large and the idea of programmable analogue quantum simulation is original.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch) supplied the key theoretical proposal for the Bose-Hubbard realisation; Bloch led the experimental programme, including the 2002 Mott transition experiment and microscopy; Esslinger realised the fermionic Hubbard model and Fermi-surface and transport studies. Greiner is also credited and did the Mott transition and the first fermionic quantum gas microscope, so choosing three of four involves a real judgement. Zoller also appears in other entries, which affects how the committee packages recognition.
assessment.maturity: Mature in the sense that the techniques are widely replicated; the open question is whether the physics is a decisive discovery or a method whose headline scientific results, such as solving open Hubbard-model problems, are still emerging.
uncertainties: Whether the scientific discovery component is strong enough relative to the method.
The allocation among the four credited names is contested.
Overlap with B014 and B023 involving Zoller and Cirac.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry provides inertial-sensing and fundamental-constant measurements, including determination of the fine-structure constant, gravimetry, gradiometry and tests of the equivalence principle. As a precision-instrument advance with broad scientific reach, it is the type of work I respect: an enabling measurement technology that changes what can be measured.
assessment.attribution: Bordé developed the theory of atom interferometry (including the Bordé-Ramsey geometry); Pritchard demonstrated the first matter-wave interferometers with atoms; Kasevich built the high-precision light-pulse devices and the gravity-gradient and constant measurements. Others, such as Chu, are not credited and Chu already has a 1997 prize for cooling, so the credited three can reasonably carry the prize, but Keith Hinds, Chu, Kasevich lineage and Ramsey-Bordé history are subtle.
assessment.maturity: Techniques are well established and independently replicated. Headline applications such as space-based tests and gravitational-wave detection are still developing, so some of the strongest scientific payoffs are not yet realised.
uncertainties: Priority and credit between Bordé, Pritchard, Chu and Kasevich is difficult to disentangle.
Whether the prize is for the method or for a specific discovery.
Possible overlap with prior recognised atom-optics prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The first horizon-scale images of M87* and Sgr A* from the Event Horizon Telescope are direct, visually unambiguous evidence for black-hole shadows and tests of general relativity in the strong-field regime. This is a remarkable instrument-and-analysis achievement: a planet-sized very-long-baseline interferometer at millimetre wavelengths.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed the shadow imaging concept and Doeleman led the building of the EHT array and collaboration. Moran's earlier VLBI work was also foundational. However, the result is the product of a collaboration of several hundred people, so a prize limited to three individuals is a structural problem rather than a clean attribution.
assessment.maturity: Strong confirmations: independent images of two black holes, multi-epoch and polarisation results. The interpretation is stable, though the ring size and spin inferences depend on modelling assumptions. Recognition is timely, although the 2020 prize already honoured black-hole theory and the Galactic Centre.
uncertainties: Collaboration-scale credit cannot be fairly captured by three names.
Image reconstruction and model-dependence debates remain.
Closeness to the 2020 black-hole prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson at the LHC by ATLAS and CMS confirmed the final missing particle of the Standard Model, a landmark in fundamental physics and instrumentation. The 2013 prize recognised the theory, so the experimental side remains unrecognised. The detectors and analysis represent decades of particle-physics experiment engineering, which I know well from my own CERN background.
assessment.attribution: Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee were the founders and early leaders of the ATLAS and CMS proposals; Gianotti was the ATLAS spokesperson at the 2012 announcement; Evans led the LHC machine. Any three-person allocation overlooks the thousands of members of the collaborations and excludes some of the other named people, so fairness is a serious obstacle under Nobel statutes.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently confirmed by two experiments; the coupling measurements continue to improve. The timing is arguably overdue, but the statutes make the award structurally hard.
uncertainties: The three-person rule versus the collaboration scale makes fair attribution difficult.
The committee already awarded the theory in 2013, so it may regard the question as closed.
The choice among founders, spokespersons and the machine builder is a judgement I cannot resolve from the supplied credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Silicon pixel and microstrip detectors for precision tracking made it possible to reconstruct vertices in heavy-quark and Higgs physics, and underpin the LHC experiments. From my experimental-instrument perspective, this is a quiet but decisive enabling technology whose impact on particle physics across decades is hard to overstate.
assessment.attribution: Parker developed the early microstrip and pixel concepts and Heijne led hybrid pixel detector development at CERN, while Snoeys contributed the monolithic and readout-electronics side. The field also includes Kemmer's silicon planar technology and Rossi, which are not credited, so priorities in pixel detectors are spread across several groups.
assessment.maturity: The technology is mature and widely used. The question is whether the Nobel committee views an instrument as a discovery in itself; the prize has recognised such tools (for example, the multiwire proportional chamber) but sparingly.
uncertainties: Credit is spread across many developers and may not match the three credited names.
Whether a detector technology rather than a discovery fits the prize criteria.
Closeness to the Charpak precedent for detectors.
